video_title: Elizabeth Warren Gets Another Shot at Crypto
gist: Paradigm senior adviser and former Democratic staffer Justin Slaughter tells Bankless that after the November 2026 Democratic sweep (260 House / 56 Senate seats) crypto faces a tougher but not existential two years: broad congressional oversight of tech, AI, crypto and corporate America led by angry senior members, Elizabeth Warren back as Senate Banking chair, and a less crypto-friendly Maxine Waters market-structure bill, offset by Trump-appointed SEC/CFTC leadership, a younger crypto-literate freshman class, and Hyperliquid-style TradFi convergence. He argues the decisive crypto fight is the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, not Congress.

insights.claim: After winning large majorities (about 260 House seats and 56 Senate seats), congressional Democrats plan broad oversight spanning tech, crypto, AI, prediction markets, meat/agriculture, tariff refunds, China, and private equity rollups, so crypto is one target among many rather than the sole focus.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: A diffuse 'everything is a priority' oversight agenda dilutes regulatory headline risk for any single sector, including crypto.
insights.quote: the idea is to do oversight of anything in tech, anything in crypto, anything in AI, anything in prediction markets

insights.claim: Slaughter expects Nvidia to be one of three or four primary early oversight targets based on current events.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Watch for congressional letters/hearings as a headline-risk catalyst for NVDA.

insights.claim: Expected crypto oversight topics include the SEC enforcement cases dismissed under Trump, token exchanges, World Liberty Financial, and any entity connected to a presidential pardon.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Trump-linked crypto entities and firms whose SEC cases were dropped carry elevated headline and legal risk through 2027.

insights.claim: Congressional oversight capacity is constrained: the US Senate only got access to Claude in October 2026 (previously relying on Microsoft Office's AI tool), and Slaughter recalls committees producing roughly one oversight letter every three days, so the feared weekly CEO hearings are unrealistic.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Bandwidth limits mean oversight will be noisier than it is damaging; discount threats of mass CEO testimony.
insights.quote: The entire US Senate got clawed in October for the first time ever.

insights.claim: The key internal Democratic debate is whether Trump is a unique aberration or a symptom of broader neoliberal 'rot'; if the latter view wins, oversight targets 'anybody and everybody' rather than only Trump-linked companies, and that fight plays out over the next six months.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Track which faction dominates caucus messaging to gauge whether sector-wide corporate oversight risk is rising.
insights.quote: If it's Trump as a symptom, it could be on anybody and everybody.

insights.claim: Slaughter expects the oversight sequence to run from broad voluntary-response letters, to company-specific follow-ups under subpoena threat, to depositions, investigations and reports, but doubts it yields many truly damaging crypto hearings.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Letters are early-stage signals; escalation to subpoenas is the point where company-specific risk becomes material.

insights.claim: Senior Democratic members and staff are more angry at corporate America than at Trump, feeling betrayed by companies and law firms that cooperated with or settled with the Trump administration; those law firms are likely early oversight targets.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Companies seen as close to the Trump administration face reputational/oversight risk under Democratic committee chairs.

insights.claim: Slaughter predicts aggressive corporate oversight will not materially lower prices, so with Congress following polls it will be curtailed over the following 18 months, while supply-side moves like the permitting bill or repealing the Jones Act are the real price levers.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Expect oversight intensity to peak early in 2027 and fade; supply-side permitting reforms may matter more for markets.

themes.theme: Warren, Waters and the next market-structure bill

insights.claim: Elizabeth Warren becomes Senate Banking Committee chair, but her influence in the Democratic Party is weaker than in 2021 after her reputation dimmed during the Biden administration; the next six months are a test of whether she still runs Democratic economic policy.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Warren's success or failure at setting the agenda signals how hostile Democratic financial regulation will be for crypto and banks.
insights.quote: does Elizabeth Warren still run economic policy in the Democratic party.

insights.claim: Warren publicly said crypto has had 18 years to show a positive use case and it is hard to see one, signalling continued hostility from the incoming banking chair.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Warren (quoted by host)
insights.so_what: Senate Banking under Warren is unlikely to advance crypto-friendly legislation.
insights.quote: They've had 18 years now to show the positive use case for crypto and it's hard to see where that is.

insights.claim: Slaughter does not expect Warren to pursue a crypto bill; instead incoming House Financial Services chair Maxine Waters is drafting one that is less friendly than CLARITY, likely weakening BRCA, getting tougher on DeFi, and giving the SEC more rulemaking power relative to the CFTC.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: A Waters bill would shift jurisdiction toward the SEC and raise DeFi compliance burdens; DeFi protocols and developers are most exposed.
insights.quote: there's in particular going to be some risk that BRCA is substantially weakened and much tougher on DeFi.

insights.claim: The Waters bill is also expected to include provisions the industry can accept, such as monthly attestation of stablecoin reserves, 24-hour payout requirements, and more segregation of functions (the last being more troublesome).
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuers already doing monthly attestations face limited incremental cost; function segregation could hit vertically integrated exchanges.

insights.claim: Banks will try to use renewed legislation to re-litigate stablecoin yield; Slaughter suggests crypto split community banks from big banks by allowing stablecoin yield conditional on holding some deposits at community banks.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: The stablecoin yield fight is unresolved and a key risk to yield-bearing stablecoin models; a community-bank deposit compromise is a plausible landing zone.

insights.claim: Crypto industry negotiators erred by working mainly with Republicans and walking away from CLARITY talks in September; Senator Ruben Gallego's 'talk to Sherrod Brown' remark signals Democratic frustration at that walk-away.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Market-structure legislation now requires broad Democratic buy-in and more concessions than before.

insights.claim: With Paul Atkins at the SEC and Mike Selig at the CFTC, Democrats control Congress but not the regulators, so the agencies will keep advancing crypto rules; however, the main congressional danger is appropriations riders barring specific rulemakings, which Slaughter thinks unlikely for crypto.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Agency-level crypto-friendly rulemaking likely continues through 2027; watch appropriations bills for riders.

insights.claim: Rules finalized in the last year of an administration can be reversed via the Congressional Review Act (as with SAB 121), and rules typically take about a year from proposal to final, so Trump-era crypto rules started now may not all survive a 2029 change in administration.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Regulatory wins finalized late in 2027-2028 are fragile; legislation offers more durable protection than agency rules.

insights.claim: Funding fights, including over funding the Iran war, could leave the SEC and CFTC funded for only 60-90 days of the year, materially harming regulatory action.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Government-shutdown risk could stall ETF approvals and crypto rulemakings in 2027.

insights.claim: Slaughter does not expect a crypto-driven financial crisis that would trigger 2009-style mass legislation, citing DeFi functioning perfectly during the November 2022 collapse as evidence of code quality.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Tail risk of punitive crisis-driven crypto legislation is low absent an exogenous blow-up.
insights.quote: DeFi functioned perfectly in November of 22.

themes.theme: Crypto voter politics and the 2028 primary

insights.claim: Data Slaughter cites show crypto owners went from 4% more Democratic than the country in 2020 to 13% more Republican in 2024, a 17-point swing and the biggest of any group; he warns Democrats now dismissing the single-issue crypto voter will repeat the mistake.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Renewed regulatory hostility could re-mobilize crypto owners against Democrats, a political constraint on anti-crypto policy.

insights.claim: Crypto single-issue voters were roughly 2% of independents and 5% of voters in 2024, there is no anti-crypto single-issue voter, but there is now an anti-data-center single-issue voter with evidence that data centers swung elections.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Data-center buildout is becoming a local political liability, a risk for AI infrastructure siting and hyperscaler capex.
insights.quote: There is, I think, now an anti-s single issue data center voter.

insights.claim: Super PAC spending (e.g., Fairshake) showed limited effectiveness in 2026; Fairshake's deliberate choice to spend only in Ohio and Nebraska avoided full partisan alignment and helped the industry.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Crypto political money is less of a lever than assumed; macro anger beats PAC dollars.
insights.quote: a super PAC can't beat a wave.

insights.claim: A large Democratic majority is better for crypto than a narrow one because it brings in young, moderate, non-white freshmen without stakes in old fights (e.g., James Talarico, who voted for a Texas Bitcoin fund), and the crypto divide is primarily generational (under ~45s are crypto-literate).
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Generational turnover structurally favors crypto policy over time.
insights.quote: I think the big Democratic victory was a lot better than narrow one.

insights.claim: The decisive crypto policy fight is the 2028 Democratic presidential primary; most likely candidates are not anti-crypto (one or two are), and Slaughter expects the nominee to treat Biden-era crypto policy as a huge error. Major candidates likely announce in February-March 2027.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Candidate positioning in early 2027 is the leading indicator for 2029+ crypto regulatory regime.
insights.quote: The real fight for the Democrats on crypto is not even going to happen in Congress.

insights.claim: Slaughter predicts AOC will not run for president in 2028 and will instead run successfully for the Senate in New York, for personal reasons.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Narrows the progressive field for 2028.

insights.claim: Slaughter grades the crypto industry as having had a good first two years under Trump that will be followed by two less good years, and says a Harris win would have meant less good first two years but less bad later years.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for a tougher crypto policy backdrop through 2028 versus 2025-2026.
insights.quote: Crypto had a good first two years. These next two years will not be as good.

themes.theme: Use cases and TradFi convergence narrative

insights.claim: Hyperliquid's use for pricing oil over a weekend in February is gaining traction on Capitol Hill as a use case, and Slaughter argues 24/7 on-chain trading removes the ability to time military actions for weekends when markets are closed.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: 24/7 on-chain derivatives on real-world assets are a credible policy-facing narrative supporting Hyperliquid adoption.
insights.quote: A world where 24/7 trading happens on hyperlquid is a world where you can't do that.

insights.claim: Slaughter is closely watching pending Hyperliquid approvals, which he views as a major moment representing the true, lasting merger of crypto and TradFi.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Approval of Hyperliquid-related products would be a regulatory catalyst for HYPE and on-chain perps venues.

insights.claim: Austin Campbell's Odd Lots appearance shifted Joe Weisenthal toward seeing blockchain value, an example of 'blockchain not Bitcoin' arguments now gaining credibility in Washington and finance media.
insights.speaker: host / Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Mainstream finance media sentiment shift supports institutional on-chain adoption narratives.

insights.claim: Slaughter's risk scenario is the 'ghettoization of crypto': stablecoins and on-chain securities rails win adoption while Washington declares them 'not crypto,' keeping the crypto label toxic.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Value may accrue to tokenization and stablecoin rails rather than native crypto tokens if this framing wins.
insights.quote: This would be the ghettoization of crypto

insights.claim: Much Democratic financial-regulatory skepticism of crypto stems from 2008 and swaps deregulation; crypto was the first new financial innovation after the crisis, and Slaughter argues anything surviving a second bubble is persistent and can only be channeled, citing Europe's MiCA as proof it can be regulated.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Expect Democratic regulators to frame crypto rules through systemic-risk lenses; the persistence argument supports a long-term regulated-industry outcome.
insights.quote: So much of the fight over crypto is really a fight about 2008.

insights.claim: Crypto's benefits (cheaper payments, cross-border transfers, payroll) mostly accrue to small businesses, investors and people without dollar access rather than W-2 suburban voters, which is why many Democrats don't see the use case; Slaughter expects securities markets to move onto crypto rails, making the debate moot.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Tokenized securities settlement is the adoption vector most likely to normalize crypto politically.

insights.claim: The Senate Democrats' proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10% is highly popular on first-order polling but would cut credit availability; Slaughter warns the most dangerous faction understands it cuts credit and wants that outcome.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Rate-cap legislation is a tail risk for card issuers and subprime lenders under the new Congress.
